sources.title: Use of satellite imagery to estimate distribution and abundance of Cumberland Sound beluga whales reveals frequent use of a glacial river estuary
sources.authors: Amanda M. Belanger; Bryanna A. H. Sherbo; James D. Roth; Cortney A. Watt
sources.evidence_kind: Original research article; actually read HTML prose only.
sources.actual_read_scope: Publisher identity, introduction, methods, discussion sections4.1–4.2 and rights/data-availability statements; Figure1 acquisition failed and no figure pixels were read.
sources.observation: The authors identify Ranger River as carrying Penny Ice Cap meltwater into the Millut Bay estuary of Clearwater Fiord. They distinguish a smaller river offshoot toward Shilmilik Bay. These are regional naming facts, not correspondence for the selected inland route or terminal.
sources.source_independence: This University of Manitoba/DFO study analyzed WorldView images collected in2020–2022 for beluga distribution. Its own research identity is distinct from the held geological, hydrographic-navigation and historical publications; no borrowed or unseen map was used.
sources.limits: Prose cannot identify every selected ice/rock/lake/river passage or distinguish the actual selected terminal branch. No current hydrological, navigational or registry conclusion.
sources.use_notice: Article CC BY; Maxar imagery has separate copyright and distribution restrictions. Only own factual synthesis is delivered.

correspondence.finding: The chosen opening lies on a mapped eastern tributary approaching Bear Creek. Blue stream linework continues west from the opening to its junction with the northward Bear Creek valley. The generalized initial bends remain in that same feeder corridor; no lake, glacier, divide crossing or unshown through-link is required.

After the eastern feeder joins, the selected path turns northwest along the repeatedly labeled Bear Creek valley and then north into the southeastern arm of Becharof Lake. The creek, intermediate tributary entries and its actual lake entry are continuously depicted. Salmon Creek, Cleo Creek and Becharof Creek are separately mapped neighboring tributaries rather than substituted names for this chosen feeder.

The selected route enters the southeastern arm and continues through the large, continuously connected Becharof Lake toward its northwestern outlet. The island-rich arm, opening into the main lake, long southern-side lake traverse and diagonal approach to the outlet are all visible. Generalized lake lines clip shoreline details and islands; they do not establish a surveyed navigable track. The lake remains a separately named water body, even where river labels are rendered across its surface.

The lake narrows at its northwestern outlet into a continuously mapped Egegik River reach, then widens into a lagoon-like river reach and narrows again downstream. Original linework and repeated Egegik labels establish this lake-to-river passage and the ensuing northwestern turn. The source does not depict a dam or managed transfer along this selected outlet.

The selected corridor follows the labeled Egegik River past the Shosky Creek entry, downstream bends and island-divided lower reaches toward Egegik settlement. All intervening selected parts lie in the same depicted connected river corridor. The route passes the Egg Island setting before approaching the broad King Salmon River junction.

The selected terminal turns north from lower Egegik River toward the eastern margin of the King Salmon River mouth beside King Salmon Island. The original map shows the broad joined waters and marsh-edge setting continuously. The selected endpoint is therefore described as the Egegik–King Salmon confluence margin; it is not an independently established open-coast or seaward Egegik Bay endpoint. The north-turning terminal segment does not establish downstream flow direction in the King Salmon arm.

Becharof Lake is the substantive selected lake passage. Ruth Lake and its outlet lie south of the chosen Bear Creek approach and are not traversed by this selection. The inspected chosen route shows no selected glacier, reservoir, canal or managed diversion. The lower widened river and marsh-margin terminal are accounted for explicitly; nearby lakes and tributaries are not treated as extra selected transfers.

correspondence.component_scope: Chosen northern opening and south-then-west approach in the Sabanalarga setting.
correspondence.finding: Municipal prose distinguishes several tributaries and their receivers, including Cajón–Platanal and Molinero/Isabel López relationships. It does not locate the selected opening continuously; none of those names is assigned to it.

correspondence.component_scope: Eastern reservoir-vicinity continuation and southwestward turn.
correspondence.finding: The Guájaro field-study location and bathymetry figures show the reservoir’s elongated northern body and broader southern sector. They support the regional reservoir setting, but their inspected detail does not establish every selected through-link or the initial entry.

correspondence.component_scope: Southward continuation from the reservoir vicinity toward the canal/wetland belt.
correspondence.finding: The field-study prose identifies El Limón and Villa Rosa as the two regulated Guájaro–Canal del Dique connections. That relationship does not by itself establish which connection, if either, the selected southward line represents.

correspondence.component_scope: Long southwestern continuation across the middle lowland toward the lower delta setting.
correspondence.finding: The cultural nomination describes the artificial canal and connected wetland environment. No inspected primary cartography establishes this selected diagonal as a continuous canal, named river, or complete chain of lake/wetland connectors.

correspondence.component_scope: Westward lower continuation and actual selected coastal terminal.
correspondence.finding: The nomination distinguishes the Cartagena outlet, the Matunilla and Lequerica outlets to Barbacoas, and Correa to the Caribbean. Corchal planning prose identifies the nearby coastal lagoon/channel network. Those regional descriptions do not establish the chosen branch and its full westward approach; the model’s sea class is not independent mouth evidence.

correspondence.component_scope: Chosen western opening and initial eastward reach
correspondence.finding: This initial reach is outside the independently inspected Erichsen Lake map. The opening, any small-waterbody passages and the first eastward link have no original-source correspondence in this pass.

correspondence.component_scope: Northward turn, northern bend and returning southeastward links
correspondence.finding: The selected bends remain west of the inspected map boundary. No original evidence establishes their connecting channel, any intervening ponds or lakes, or a river name.

correspondence.component_scope: Eastward middle route and connection into the lower mapped valley
correspondence.finding: The east end of part18, using one-based part numbering, reaches the map's western edge in the broad lower Gifford valley. Most of this component is outside the map. The western through-link into that visible reach remains unestablished; a downstream name alone cannot fill it.

correspondence.component_scope: Map-edge entry, broad braided valley and approach to Asta Lake
correspondence.finding: The selected eastern course follows the map's broad, multichannel valley labeled Gifford River. The map shows continuous blue channels through the bends and the intervening tributary junctions toward the lake approach. Ordinary valley and channel correspondence is established without selecting a precise contemporary braid or bank.

correspondence.component_scope: River entrance, Asta Lake passage and downstream outlet
correspondence.finding: The broad lower river enters the northwestern end of the lake labeled Asta Lake and continues from its southeastern end into the same descending valley. The selected passage and its short adjoining part correspond to this river–lake–river connection. Asta is the lake's printed label, not a second name imposed on the whole selected river.

correspondence.component_scope: Asta outlet, lower river and head of Gifford Fiord
correspondence.finding: A continuous channel descends from Asta Lake past mapped rapid symbols and opens into the northwestern head of Gifford Fiord. The selected final parts follow this corridor and end at that river-to-fiord transition. The terminal is the fiord head, rather than a farther seaward place. No glacier or managed-water connector is needed for this inspected lower section.

No independent source pixels establish the chosen northeastern opening or its initial westward and southward terrain succession. The regional Penny Ice Cap reference does not locate this selected opening.

The selected upper westward traverse, its bends and adjoining ice, rock or water intervals remain uninspected in independent cartography. No continuous terrain correspondence or natural-river identity is inferred from the modeled trace.

The selected southwestward descent, westward reach and subsequent southern turn lack independent readable through-link material. A regional source-to-estuary statement cannot supply these particular joins.

The southward descent and western excursion remain materially unestablished. Any intervening lake, ice-margin, exposed-rock or river passage would need ordinary source correspondence; none is assumed from line shape.

The lower southeastward/southward approach lacks inspected source cartography. The literature identifies a main Ranger River input and a separate smaller offshoot, so a nearby named estuary cannot select the actual branch.

The supplied source endpoint and the rendered endpoint are distinct. Their vicinity and the final southward extension have no inspected independent pixels. Neither point is treated as a surveyed river mouth; the receiving bay for the actual selected extension remains unconfirmed.
